India Women Reach Commonwealth Kabaddi Semifinals After Beating Nigeria

India's women defeated Nigeria 38-10 to reach the Commonwealth Kabaddi semifinals, while the men's team also dominated their Nigerian opponents.

By LokkeeVerse · 2 min read

India's women's kabaddi team secured a semifinal place at the inaugural Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship with a 38-10 victory over Nigeria in Ahmedabad, according to Lokmat Times. The publisher also reported a dominant Indian men's performance against Nigeria. For Nigerian readers, the results highlight the challenge of facing an established kabaddi powerhouse and raise questions about how international competition can support the sport's development at home.

India's Women Move Into the Knockout Stage

The women's result delivered a clear competitive milestone: qualification for the semifinals. India's 28-point winning margin indicates a decisive contest, although the score alone does not establish which players, raids or defensive sequences shaped the outcome. The next stage shifts attention from securing qualification to handling the pressure of knockout competition.

India has a long-established kabaddi tradition, with extensive domestic competition and experience at major international events. That background provides useful context for its strength without explaining every detail of this match. Lokmat Times also described the Indian men as dominant against Nigeria, but the women's confirmed semifinal berth remains the clearest tournament consequence of the reported results.

What the Results Mean for Nigerian Kabaddi

Kabaddi combines short attacking raids with coordinated team defence. A raider enters the opposing half seeking points through touches before returning safely, while defenders try to stop that return. Success depends on timing, agility, communication and decisions made under pressure. A wide scoreline can reflect advantages across several of these areas, rather than a single weakness.

For Nigeria, matches against experienced opponents can offer a demanding benchmark. Their longer-term value depends on whether lessons feed into coaching, regular training and meaningful domestic competition. One result should not be treated as a complete assessment of a national programme. The more useful questions concern how consistently players compete and what support exists to turn international exposure into improvement.

  • India's women beat Nigeria 38-10 and advanced to the semifinals.
  • Lokmat Times also reported Indian men's dominance against Nigeria.
  • India's established kabaddi system provides context for its competitive strength.
  • Nigeria's development will require more than occasional tournament appearances.

Readers should watch for India's semifinal opponent and subsequent knockout results, alongside confirmation of the men's score and tournament position. For Nigeria, the next fixtures and any concrete plans for coaching, player development or domestic competition will offer a better measure of progress than this defeat alone.
